detail.introHeading: A-level Maths tutoring from a teacher of nearly 40 years
intro: A-level Maths builds on itself. A gap in algebra from Year 12 shows up again in calculus, in mechanics and in statistics, and it costs marks on every paper. Tania finds where the understanding stops, explains the principle underneath, and then practises it on exam questions from your own board until it is secure.

Tania: Tania has taught A-level Maths and Further Maths for nearly 40 years, and still teaches at a top sixth form college, where she is very popular with her students.

She has a deep understanding of how students take in mathematics and of the best ways to help them learn. Parents and students most often mention how clearly she explains the reasoning behind each step.

detail.focusHeading: Where marks are won and lost in A-level Maths

focus.p: Algebra and functions is the most heavily examined area of the Edexcel specification, with more marks since 2018 than trigonometry, differentiation or integration. Slips in algebra are also how marks are lost in every other topic, so it is usually the first thing to secure.

These ask for the reasoning to be written out, not just a correct answer. Examiners report that students often cannot set up a proof by contradiction in the right language, leaving out words such as “assume”. It is a skill that improves quickly with practice.

focus.h: Statistics and the large data set
focus.p: Statistics questions expect a conclusion written in the context of the question, and both boards expect students to know their large data set. Hypothesis tests follow the same steps every time, and marks are lost when one of those steps is missing.

Kinematics and forces carry a large share of the applied marks. Many errors come before any calculation: a missing force on the diagram, or a sign going the wrong way. Tania teaches students to set a problem up carefully so the working follows.

detail.focusHeading: Where marks are won and lost in A-level Further Maths

focus.h: The hardest parts of Core Pure
focus.p: The topics students most often ask Emma for are proof by induction, complex loci, hyperbolic functions and second-order differential equations. Each has a method that can be learned and a way of setting out the answer that the mark scheme expects.

Every Edexcel student sits Core Pure and then two option papers, chosen from Further Pure, Further Statistics, Further Mechanics and Decision. Schools usually choose for the whole class. Emma teaches all of them, so lessons follow the options your school has entered you for.

Further Maths questions rely on fluent algebra, calculus and trigonometry from A-level Maths. When a Further Maths answer goes wrong, the cause is often there. Emma teaches both courses, so she can go back and fix it.

There are four papers of an hour and a half each, and time is tight on all of them. In the final term, lessons often work through full papers under timed conditions and then go over where marks were dropped.

detail.focusHeading: Where marks are won and lost in A-level Biology

focus.p: Many questions describe an experiment or an organism the student has never seen and ask them to use what they know. Students who have only learned their notes find these hard. Every lesson works through real past-paper questions for the student’s board.

Biology mark schemes look for particular terms and ideas. An answer can show understanding and still miss the mark because a key word is missing. Lessons show what each mark is given for, so students learn to write what earns it.

At least 10% of the marks in A-level Biology need maths, and practical skills are examined in the written papers. Calculations, graphs, statistical tests and questions on method can all be practised until they are reliable.

Each board has longer written questions, including the 25-mark essay on AQA Paper 3 and the six-mark level-of-response questions on OCR A. They reward planning and a clear structure as much as knowledge.

detail.introHeading: A-level Chemistry tutoring built around the exam
intro: A-level Chemistry is really three subjects: physical, inorganic and organic. Most students are stronger in one than the others, and the exam papers mix all three. Lessons start by finding which topics and question types are costing marks, then work through them using questions from your own exam board’s past papers.

Laraib: Laraib is a practising medical doctor who has tutored A-level Chemistry for eight years, with more than a thousand hours of online lessons. She achieved 11 A*s at GCSE and A*AAA at A level, and has over 60 five-star reviews from students and parents.

She explains each topic until it is properly understood before moving on. She sets homework after every lesson, uses regular assessments to show what is secure and what needs more work, and gives parents progress updates whenever they ask.

detail.focusHeading: Where marks are won and lost in A-level Chemistry

focus.p: Amount of substance is the most-examined topic on all three boards: 291 question parts on OCR A, 358 on AQA and 361 on Edexcel since 2016. At least 20% of the marks in A-level Chemistry need maths. Laraib teaches students to set out every step, so the method marks are safe even when the final answer slips.

A curly arrow has to start and finish in exactly the right place to score. Students practise each mechanism on their specification until they can draw it the way the mark scheme expects, then move on to synthesis routes that join several reactions together.

Every board sets extended questions that are marked by levels, not point by point. On OCR A there are two on every A-level paper. Students learn to answer every strand of the question in a logical order, which is the difference between a middle-level and a top-level answer.

Practical work is examined in the written papers: OCR’s practical activity groups, AQA’s required practicals and Edexcel’s core practicals. Questions on method, sources of error and improving an experiment come up every series, and they can be prepared for.

detail.focusHeading: Where marks are won and lost in A-level Physics

focus.p: Mark schemes give marks for each step and allow an error to be carried forward, but a wrong answer with no working earns nothing. Rosey teaches students to set out every step, with units, so the method marks are safe.

Practical work is examined in the written papers. Measurements and uncertainties is the most-examined topic in our AQA question bank, and practical skills is the most-examined on OCR A. These questions follow patterns that can be learned.
Some marks depend on a definition given exactly as the examiners expect it, and “explain” questions need each step of the reasoning written down. Lessons practise the wording as well as the physics.
Each board sets longer written questions that are marked by levels. Students learn to plan a short, ordered answer that covers every part of the question, which is what reaches the top level.

detail.introHeading: A-level Psychology tutoring from a former AQA examiner
intro: A-level Psychology rewards three different skills: knowing the content, applying it to an unfamiliar scenario, and evaluating it. Students who revise the content alone often find their marks stall. Andy has examined for AQA, and each lesson covers a topic in full and then puts it to work on exam questions, which he marks and goes over.

Andy: Andy has taught A-level Psychology for nearly 30 years in top sixth form colleges. AQA is his specialism and he has been an AQA examiner, though he can teach every exam board.
He has a reputation for lessons that get to the point: the knowledge a question needs, the evaluation that reaches the top band, and how to use the scenario in application questions.

detail.focusHeading: Where marks are won and lost in A-level Psychology

focus.p: Research methods is the most-examined area of the course: 445 of the 1,208 AQA question parts in our question bank since 2016. It includes the maths, from choosing a statistical test to interpreting significance, and it is where many students drop marks they could keep.

A 16-mark essay is about 20 minutes of writing, and the top level needs evaluation that is developed, not just listed. Evaluation that only describes stays in the lower levels. Andy marks essays the way an examiner does and shows what would lift each one.

Many questions give a short scenario and ask students to apply what they know to it. Marks are lost when the answer is correct psychology but never mentions the scenario. Lessons practise using the details in the question, line by line.

AQA updated the Psychology specification for first A-level exams in June 2027. The papers and question types are the same, but some content has been removed or reworded. Andy teaches to the current specification, so revision time is not spent on material that has gone.

detail.introHeading: A-level Economics tutoring from a former Edexcel examiner
intro: In A-level Economics, understanding the theory is only the start. The higher grades come from applying it to the data in front of you, building a chain of reasoning, and evaluating it. Liane has examined for Edexcel, and she sets essays every week, marks them, and goes through them in the next lesson.

Liane: Liane taught A-level Economics for over twenty years, as Head of Department in a school rated outstanding by Ofsted and in an outstanding sixth form college. She has been an examiner for Edexcel A-level Economics and A-level Business.
Each lesson covers a topic in full, then moves to real past-paper questions, which she marks against the Edexcel levels grids and goes over with the student.

detail.focusHeading: Where marks are won and lost in A-level Economics

focus.p: Section C of each A-level paper offers a choice of two 25-mark essays, about 30 minutes of writing. The top level needs chains of reasoning, relevant diagrams and evaluation that reaches a judgement.

A diagram earns marks when it is accurate, fully labelled and then used in the argument. Students often draw the right diagram and never refer to it. Liane teaches how to make each one do some work in the answer.

The data-response questions in Section B give marks for application: using the figures and the context in the extracts. An answer that would fit any economy or any firm misses those marks, however good the theory.

Section A is where easy marks leak away through a missing definition, a calculation without working, or a diagram with no labels. A reliable technique for these questions protects marks before the essays begin.

focus.p: The 10-mark “applying material from the Item” questions and most of the essays come with an Item. The top bands need the Item’s points picked up and developed alongside the student’s own knowledge. Ignoring it, or copying it out, keeps an answer in the middle.

Papers 1 and 3 each end in a 30-mark essay, about 45 minutes of writing. Listing studies is not enough: the top level asks for analysis and for evaluation that reaches a judgement. Mark teaches a structure students can rely on under time pressure.

This 20-mark question has appeared on every Paper 1 since 2017. It asks students to apply a research method to a particular issue in education. Answers that describe the method in general, without tying it to the issue, are held in the middle bands.

Theory and Methods is examined on both Paper 1 and Paper 3, so it carries more marks than any single topic. Lessons link the theories to the topics students already know, which makes them easier to remember and to use in essays.

focus.p: Many questions come with a map, graph, table or photograph: on Edexcel they sit in a separate Resource Booklet. Marks are given for using that data precisely, quoting figures and spotting patterns and exceptions, not for describing it in general terms.

The longest questions on both boards are worth 20 marks and are marked by levels. On AQA alone, 153 have been set since 2017. The top level needs a sustained argument and a conclusion that answers the question, not a list of everything the student knows.

Edexcel’s Paper 3 is a synoptic investigation: an unseen issue, with a booklet of resources, that draws on the whole course. It rewards students who can link physical and human geography under time pressure, and it can be practised.

The independent investigation is worth 20% of the A level on both boards. The boards limit how much help a teacher or tutor may give, and our tutors work within those rules: helping students plan, choose methods and understand what the mark scheme is looking for.

intro: A-level English Language and English Literature are both marked on the quality of the argument, not the amount written. detail.focusHeading: Where marks are won and lost in A-level English

focus.p: Top-band answers look closely at particular words, structures and patterns and name them accurately. General comments about a writer’s “effect on the reader” stay in the middle bands. Lessons practise analysis on the kinds of text the papers set.

Context earns marks when it helps explain what a text means or why it was written that way. A paragraph of background added on to the end of an essay does not. Isobel shows students how to weave it into the argument.
In Literature, students are expected to consider other interpretations. The marks come from weighing them against their own reading, not from listing what critics have said.

The Literature Paper 1 exam is three hours long, and the Language papers are two and a half. A few minutes spent planning each answer is what keeps an argument on course. Lessons include essay planning and timed writing.

intro: A-level Law tests three things: knowing the law accurately, applying it to a set of facts, and evaluating it. Students who learn the cases but have not practised applying them often find the scenario questions cost them most. Sue is a qualified solicitor who has taught A-level Law for 25 years, and her lessons are built around what the mark schemes reward.

detail.focusHeading: Where marks are won and lost in A-level Law

focus.p: The knowledge marks go to law that is stated accurately and supported by cases and statutes. A rule without its authority earns less. Lessons build a reliable set of cases for each topic and practise using them.

focus.h: Applying the law to a scenario
focus.p: Scenario questions ask students to apply the law to each person in a set of facts and reach a conclusion. Answers that explain the law well but never apply it to the people in the scenario miss the application marks.

The essay questions reward evaluation that is developed and stays focused on the question. Listing criticisms is not enough. Sue teaches students to build each point into an argument and come to a view.

focus.h: Long scenario questions against the clock
focus.p: The longest questions have to be planned and written quickly. Timed practice, marked against the levels of response, shows students how much they can cover and what to put first.

detail.focusHeading: Where marks are won and lost in GCSE Science

focus.p: The practical work students do in class is examined in the written papers. Questions ask about the method, the variables, sources of error and how to improve an experiment. Going back over each required practical is one of the quickest ways to pick up marks.

All three sciences include calculations, from moles and concentrations in Chemistry to the equations in Physics. Students lose marks by not showing working, missing units or rearranging incorrectly. Sam teaches a routine for setting them out.

The longer written questions are marked by levels, so a well-organised answer scores more than a list of facts. Students learn to plan a short answer that covers every part of the question in a sensible order.

Whether a student takes separate sciences or Combined Science, there is a lot to keep on top of. Regular weekly lessons through Year 10 and Year 11 deal with each topic while it is fresh, so revision is not left to the last few weeks.
